name: Fitts's Law
description: The time to acquire a target is a function of the distance to it and its size — smaller, more distant targets take longer to hit accurately.
design_relevance_note: Directly informs touch-target sizing, button placement, and click-path design — one of the most direct, literal applications of psychology research to interface design in this entire corpus.
prevalence_note: One of the single most-cited laws in interaction design specifically — target size and distance are a standard part of any UI design curriculum.

findings.description: The time required to rapidly move to and acquire a target is a logarithmic function of the distance-to-target-width ratio — smaller or more distant targets reliably take longer to hit accurately.
findings.source_title: The information capacity of the human motor system in controlling the amplitude of movement

applications.title: Google's centered search box as the screen's 'prime pixel' target
applications.description: Applying Fitts's Law to web design via the 'prime pixel' concept (the on-screen location a user's cursor is most likely resting at, and 'magic pixels' at the four screen corners which have effectively infinite target size but are the least useful default location for real actions): Google places its search box at the center of the screen -- the default prime-pixel location before any action is taken -- making the site's single most important action the easiest one to reach.
applications.ethical_note: Placing the primary action where it's easiest to reach benefits the user directly (less effort to accomplish their actual goal) with no persuasion-vs-user-interest tension -- a straightforward efficiency application of Fitts's Law, distinct from this graph's existing 'exploit infinite target size' (macOS/Windows screen-edge menus) and 'deliberately increase finger travel' (Sephora) examples, which sit closer to the ethically mixed end of this same law's applications.

applications.title: Sephora's iPhone app requiring long finger travel to reach the Save button
applications.description: Sephora's iPhone app places its Save button in the top-right corner of the screen, far from where a thumb naturally rests during one-handed use, increasing the movement distance and time required to complete the action -- presented as a violation of Fitts's Law rather than an application of it.
applications.ethical_note: This is a usability-competence issue, not an ethics case -- there's no indication Sephora intended to make the action harder, just an apparent oversight. Graded not_applicable rather than 'unclear': this corpus's ethical_risk axis is built to grade persuasion/manipulation intent (see the Amazon/Booking.com/Etsy entries), and there's no persuasive intent to grade here at all, unlike a case where a real ethical dimension exists but can't be resolved.

applications.title: macOS and Windows placing menus/buttons at screen edges to exploit infinite target size
applications.description: macOS places application menus at the very top edge of the screen, and pre-Windows-8 Windows placed the Start button in the bottom-left corner -- both positions exploit the fact that a screen edge acts as an effectively infinite target (the cursor can't overshoot past it), reducing the precision needed to hit the target under Fitts's Law.
applications.ethical_note: Pure usability/efficiency application with no persuasion angle -- exploiting screen edges as infinite targets purely reduces the physical effort needed to reach a common action. Included as a clean, foundational illustration of Fitts's Law with no ethical complexity, in contrast to the Sephora entry in this same wave which shows the same law being violated rather than applied.
